# The association between preventive health and outpatient spending and life expectancy by income quartile

Mason S. Barnard1 and Rama M. Hagos1,2*

Abstract Background:  To describe the relationship between longevity and local access to preventive healthcare at the county level. Methods:  We used Medicare outpatient reimbursement data from the 2010 Dartmouth Health Atlas and longevity data from Chetty et al. (2016) to identify the cross-sectional associations between county longevity, access to outpatient care, and the quality of primary care. Results:  We find that the cost of outpatient care is inversely correlated with area life expectancy for individuals in the bottom income quartile. Much of this correlation is driven by men in the bottom income quartile. We also find that disaggregating a preventive care index produces significant relationships between components of the index and longevity where none were previously found. Conclusions:  These results counter prior assertions that local health costs are not associated with life expectancy. Additionally, the results also suggest that the local cost of outpatient care and the quality of that care may influence the longevity of low-income populations, especially for low-income men. Keywords:  Preventive care, Health access, Health quality, Longevity

Background Although well-studied, the relationship between health and healthcare spending is often simplified into a relationship between longevity and dollars spent. Chetty et  al.’s (2016) landmark paper uses overall Medicare reimbursements as a proxy for health access, finding no relationship between a county’s average reimbursements and life expectancy [1]. Regional comparisons across the United States likewise suggest that more health care spending shows little association with better health outcomes [2, 3]. Medicare patients in regions with high

spending use more healthcare resources but do not see any boosts to longevity or other health outcomes [2]. Similar studies suggest that among developed countries, higher overall health spending is not significantly associated with health outcomes [4]. Yet, dollars spent in different healthcare settings are not equivalent. Abundant evidence suggests that spending on preventive and maintenance care improves overall longevity and health [5], while spending on inpatient and elderly care often outweighs potential health benefits [6, 7]. Prior authors observe such a relationship in Chetty et al. (2016)’s initial results. Referencing the paper’s supplementary analysis, one commentary notes that fewer discharges for ambulatory-sensitive conditions, a key measure of primary care access, were correlated with longer life expectancy [8]. The variations in the value of spending by care type make implicit sense. Costly

The aggregated preventive care metrics may conceal potentially significant data and bias it towards certain types of care, such as diabetes—the subject of three of the six metrics used in the index. By lumping costly inpatient procedures and end of life care with cheaper, more impactful outpatient visits and surgeries, metrics of overall spending may not adequately represent the relationship between spending and health [9]. These potential issues call for more investigation into the relationship between health access and longevity. Quality of care indices may similarly obscure the ties between different types of care and longevity. Evidence connecting quality measures to better outcomes remains modest [10], with the association between care quality and health outcomes often dependent on the specific measure used and the population of patients assessed

Such aggregation, while useful, can mask significant relationships between different dimensions of care quality and health. Given the limitations of composite health metrics, this paper assesses the cross-sectional relationship between longevity and county-level preventive care spending and quality. It draws from the methodology and data originally used in Chetty et al. (2016) and nuances our understanding of the relationship between health, healthcare spending, and healthcare quality by focusing on outpatient reimbursements and preventive care.

All analyses were performed using Stata version 16 (StataCorp, College Station, TX).

Discussion Our results suggest that there is a strong, negative association at the county level between the cost of outpatient care and life expectancy for individuals in the bottom income quartile. Interestingly, we found that this association is primarily driven by men in the bottom income quartile. Previous research has shown that low-income men have poorer health outcomes and are less likely to receive health care [14, 15]. This pattern may be the result of low-income individuals rationing elective care to avoid the cost, and is reinforced by the negative association between the ambulatory-sensitive condition discharge rate and life expectancy for those in the bottom income quartile. Rationing care among low-income men

may save money in the short-term, but likely escalates both costs and mortality over time—an important finding for policymakers. Our results further suggest that certain aspects of preventive health are significantly associated with longevity. But the nature of these associations vary. Among lowincome individuals, two of our diabetes quality metrics display a positive association, indicating that quality of preventive care is linked to life expectancy, while our third metric, the percentage of individuals receiving a primary care visit, shows a negative association. The latter finding is surprising, as we would expect that seeing a doctor is associated with better health. However, it may be explained by self-selection, with healthier individuals less likely to see a physician. Among high-income individuals, all preventive care metrics were positively associated with life expectancy. This finding reinforces the

Moreover, the consistent positive relationship between these metrics, particularly the percentage of individuals receiving a primary care visit, stands in stark contrast to the results seen among the bottom quartile of the income distribution. This contrast may suggest that while lower income individuals self-select into preventive care based on underlying health, wealthier individuals do not—lending a negative association with longevity for the former and a positive association for the latter.

Conclusion Past research has found mixed results on the relationship between health spending and life expectancy. We highlight findings that show that Medicare outpatient spending and some preventative care metrics are a better approximation of the costs and quality of health maintenance and are statistically significant with life expectancy

at the county level. The importance of health spending is especially crucial in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic, where differential access to care both before and during the pandemic has impacted the health of disadvantaged communities.

Limitations As we based the methodology of this paper on Chetty et al. (2016), we acknowledge the same limitations of the original paper. Life expectancy estimates were based on extrapolations of mortality rates after age 76 and age 63 for year-specific estimates. Income for individuals ages 63 or older was measured at age 61 because of previous evidence that earnings after age 61 are less correlated with earlier earnings due to the rate of retirement. # CICERO’S APPEAL TO NATURAL LAW IN PHILIPPICS 10 AND 11

ABSTRACT This article uses Cicero’s De legibus to unlock the force of the legal arguments in Philippics 10 and 11, which justify Brutus and Cassius’ respective invasions of Macedonia and Syria by emphasizing their conformity with the ‘law of nature’. Cicero’s rhetorical challenge (1) was to persuade senatorial moderates that giving commands to the conspirators was less threatening to the Republican legal system than were Antony’s arrangements for those provinces. Drawing on his De legibus (2), which identifies a link between positive law and nature based on its capacity to distinguish justice from injustice, Cicero provides this response to his opponents’ charge that Brutus and Cassius have broken the law: (3) because of their virtue, the pair have been able to follow natural law, as Antony has destroyed the force of public law in Macedonia and Syria, but the Senate now has a chance to rebuild the positive legal order, legitimized through its connection to Brutus and Cassius’ actions.

Keywords: Cicero; Philippics 10 and 11; Brutus and Cassius; Macedonia; Syria; De legibus; right reason (recta ratio); law (lex)

Cicero’s Philippics 10 and 11 are the published versions of two speeches delivered during the war between Mark Antony and the commonwealth in early 43 B.C.1 While Decimus Junius Brutus, who had been in charge of Cisalpine Gaul, was besieged by Antony at Mutina, and consular armies were being mobilized to free him, Cicero’s attentions turned to the east.2 At the end of 44 B.C. Marcus Brutus, joint ringleader of the conspiracy against Julius Caesar, had been assigned the governorship of Crete, but had instead gone to Athens, making contact with the outgoing governor of Macedonia, Quintus Hortensius Hortalus, son of the famous rhetorician and consul of 69 B.C.3

When Gaius Antonius, Antony’s brother, arrived in the area to assume the governorship of Macedonia in January 43 B.C., Hortensius transferred his armies to Brutus instead. Soon after, Publius Vatinius, the governor of Illyricum, also joined Brutus, and their combined forces pushed Gaius Antonius into the Illyrian city of Apollonia. In early February, Brutus wrote to Rome’s Senate, explaining that he now controlled the entire region, and would proceed according to its instructions (Cic. Phil. 10.1, Ad Brut. 2.3; Livy, Per. 118; Plut. Vit. Brut. 25–6; App. B Ciu. 3.79; Dio Cass. 47.22). In the ensuing debate, Cicero urged that Brutus be officially invested with a ‘military command’ (imperium), and the Senate is usually thought to have approved this request.4

At around the same time, Publius Cornelius Dolabella, who had been consul together with Antony in 44 B.C. and was now a committed Antonian, was making the long march to his assigned province of Syria. One possible impediment to his route was the governor of Asia, Gaius Trebonius, who was a murderer of Caesar, and who was known to be hostile to Antony’s supporters. In various accounts, Dolabella captured Trebonius by surprise in the city of Smyrna, and treated him brutally: perhaps after torturing the unfortunate man for several days, he murdered him, paraded his severed head, and tossed his mangled body into the sea (see, for example, Livy, Per. 119; Vell. Pat. 2.69; App. B Ciu. 3.26; Dio Cass. 47.29). In late February or early March, this news reached Rome to general uproar, and the consul Gaius Vibius Pansa convened the Senate. Almost immediately, Dolabella was voted an official ‘enemy’ (hostis) of the res publica, and even those senators who were sympathetic to Antony supported the resolution. There was more debate, however, about whom to appoint to command the war against him. Before Cicero arose to speak, two suggestions had just been made: one, from Lucius Julius Caesar, would have appointed the consular Publius Servilius Isauricus, who had military experience but was living as a private citizen, while another would have entrusted the operation to Pansa and his colleague Aulus Hirtius. After delivering a long invective about Dolabella’s cruelty and inhumanity, Cicero laid out his objections to these proposals, which he regarded as introducing an unnecessary delay.5 Granting an ‘extraordinary command’ (imperium extraordinarium) to a ‘private citizen’ (priuatus) was out of step with Republican precedent, and had only been done when no alternative was available. The Senate in late 44 and early 43 B.C. contained a faction of senators who had been close to Antony, which regularly called for accommodation with him. One of its leaders was Calenus, who spoke against Brutus’ command and was subject to an ad hominem attack in Philippic 10.12 In early January 43 B.C. Calenus had opposed granting honours to Octavian, including those advocated by Cicero in Philippic 5, and unsuccessfully moved that an embassy be sent to Decimus Brutus as well as to Antony, thereby treating both generals alike (Phil. 5.1; Dio Cass. 46.1–29). When the embassy returned with Antony’s counter-demands at the start of February, Calenus spoke about peace (Cic. Phil. 8.11, 8.18). When the Syrian war came to be debated, moreover, he outflanked his opposition by proposing that Dolabella be declared a hostis, but then was probably responsible for the delaying tactic of entrusting the operation to the consuls. Hardliners like Calenus aside, a great number of unaffiliated senators, suspicious both of Cicero and of Antony, and who wanted a return to normality, would have had some reservations about giving official authorization to Brutus or Cassius. NATURAL LAW IN DE LEGIBVS

Like Philippics 10 and 11, Cicero’s De legibus posits the existence of a divine and unchanging law of nature, identified with ‘right reason’, which prescribes just actions and bans unjust ones. In Book 1, it is noted that ‘law is the highest reason, implanted in nature, which commands what ought to be done and prohibits the opposite’ (lex est ratio summa insita in natura, quae iubet ea, quae facienda sunt, prohibetque contraria, 1.18; cf. 1.23). In Book 2, ‘they say that law is the principal and ultimate mind of god, compelling or forbidding all things by reason’ (principem legem illam et ultimam mentem esse dicebant omnia ratione aut cogentis aut uetantis dei, 2.8). In addition, the ‘true and final law, applied to commanding and forbidding, is the right reason of highest Jupiter’ (lex uera atque princeps, apta ad iubendum et ad uetandum, ratio est recta summi Iouis, 2.10). Although De legibus dates from the 50s B.C., Cicero kept these intellectual commitments in later years; in his De officiis, composed at the end of 44 B.C., he claims that ‘nature is the source of law’ (iuris natura fons sit).18

For Cicero, natural law is applicable to human beings because they have reason, a possession in common with the gods; since the gods possess right reason, which is natural law, this law governs gods and humans alike, and invites them to attain the virtues, chiefly justice (Leg. 1.22–3). Although this was Stoic doctrine, it is doubtful that Cicero regarded it as uniquely such: he credits ‘learned men’ (doctissimis uiris) for its formulation, in whose number he must have included the ‘prudent and sharp’ (prudens et acutus) Antiochus of Asculum, under whom a young Cicero studied in Athens, and who had tried to assimilate the teachings of Plato’s Academy with those of the Stoa (1.18, 1.54). According to Cicero and his intellectual predecessors, a select few individuals, known as ‘wise men’ or ‘sages’ (sapientes), were so virtuous and rational that they had perfected reason as right reason in their own mind, and were able to conform to the law of nature.

Because Brutus is virtuous, Cicero is saying, he has no need of statutes or decrees to guide him towards justice: instead, he has apparently laid down his own law in the provinces along his route (10.12). Emphasizing Cassius’ virtue was more daunting for Cicero. In contrast to Brutus, Cassius had not established a reputation for moral excellence, but was renowned for his aggression and impetuosity.26 Before introducing Cassius in Philippic 11, Cicero admits that Brutus would have been more suitable for a Syrian command, were he not occupied elsewhere (11.26). Antony’s arrangements were so pernicious as to have ‘suppressed’ (oppressis) the ‘written laws’ (legibus scriptis) in Syria, and that Cassius followed natural law in invading the province because it was the only kind of law available to him (11.28). What is more, Cicero’s solution to the legal emergency is that Brutus and Cassius be given a legal grant of imperium by the Senate to achieve their military objectives, and the text of his formal ‘legislative proposals’ (sententiae), meant for incorporation into senatorial decrees, is published in our versions of the two speeches.28 As Cicero urges in Philippic 10, the Senate can ‘pay tribute’ (tribuere) to Brutus by giving him a proper command (10.23). Similarly, though Brutus and Cassius are said in Philippic 11 to have been ‘a Senate for themselves’ (ipse senatus sibi fuit) and to have failed to ‘wait for our decrees’ (exspectauit decreta nostra) over the preceding months, Cicero tells the Senate that Cassius’ activities must now be retrospectively ‘confirmed by your authority’ (uestra auctoritate firmentur) in a formal manner (11.27, 11.29). In Cicero’s De legibus, one of the fundamental arguments is that positive law is modelled on natural law because it can distinguish between justice and injustice, and so can provide for genuine human goods, including political stability. Continuing in this vein in Philippics 10 and 11, Cicero strongly implies that Antony’s provincial arrangements of 44 B.C. are unjust, and that they have contributed to the destruction of public law and Republican government. In this vacuum, Brutus and Cassius, being virtuous men, have acted according to natural law; to secure the foundations of the res publica, then, the Senate must decree that Brutus and Cassius have imperium in the worst-affected regions, in order that its lawmaking may truly reflect the divine law which this pair have illuminated. As Cicero’s audience realized, his real aim was not to validate Brutus and Cassius with respect to public law, but rather to validate public law with respect to Brutus and Cassius, and ultimately with respect to right reason and the law of nature.

## CONCLUSION

In defending Brutus and Cassius from the charge of illegal entry to Macedonia and Syria respectively, Cicero’s Philippics 10 and 11 claim that these generals followed a ‘law for (him)self’ (legem sibi, 10.12), the ‘holiest law’ (legem sanctissimam, 11.27), ‘right reason’ (recta : : : ratio, 11.28) and the ‘law of nature’ (lege naturae, 11.28). Attempting to persuade the Senate to grant commands to the two conspirators, Cicero could hardly have hoped to persuade the most fervent Antonians in that body. Instead, he wanted to win over those senators closely attached neither to him nor to Antony: though these men mistrusted Brutus and Cassius, they also recognized that Antony’s consulship of the previous year had brought about a chaotic situation in the provinces. In their eyes, Cicero had to prove that supporting his own friends and allies in the eastern Mediterranean was more ‘legal’ than not doing so, and potentially allowing the crisis to persist. To make his arguments, Cicero relied upon the conception of law examined in his philosophical treatise De legibus, which he continued to think about in the 40s B.C. Here, natural law, unchanging and divine, is accessible only to the sage, who is virtuous.

Positive law, applicable to cities and states, can help human beings because it is modelled on this natural law, which prescribes just actions and forbids unjust ones. Unjust statutes, without a connection to justice, are destructive to commonwealths. Given the philosophical literacy of the Roman elite in the late first century B.C., Cicero could have expected a senatorial audience to be familiar with the basic outline of these ideas. In Philippics 10 and 11, then, Cicero emphasizes the philosophical virtue of Brutus, and by extension that of Cassius, though it is harder to make the same argument in the latter’s case. Because of this virtue, he implies, they have been able to follow the lex naturae during their operations in the east, in a manner that is reminiscent of the Stoic sage. At the same time, though, he notes that they were only compelled to do so because Antony has destroyed the positive legal order with respect to Macedonia and Syria. To reconstitute it, the Senate must pass decrees which are modelled on the law of nature, in so far as they commend the actions of Brutus and Cassius. Whether or not one might be personally convinced by this philosophical tour de force—and it should be noted that Cicero’s proposal in Philippic 11 was rejected by the Senate—the two speeches are very sophisticated pieces of work, which undoubtedly merit further study.
